messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo source: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25 nF) and $R_{leak} = 20 \text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude $V_{oc} \approx 3.2 \text{ V}$.
    *   Load $R_L$: varies from 150 k$\Omega$ (S2) to 2200 k$\Omega$ (S3).
    *   Target: $V_{out}$ between 1.8 V and 3.6 V.
    *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05 \text{ V}$.
    *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4 \text{ s}$.
    *   Settled $dv \le 0.02 \text{ V}$ (stability).
    *   Operating conditions S1-S6 cover various load and source strengths.

    *   S1: Nominal.
    *   S2: Heavy load (150 k$\Omega$). FBR failed $V_{avg} \ge 1.8 \text{ V}$ and startup.
    *   S3: Strong excitation, light load (2200 k$\Omega$). FBR failed $V_{max} \le 3.6 \text{ V}$ (overvoltage), ripple, and stability.
    *   S4: Weak excitation (30 $\mu$A), heavy load (1000 k$\Omega$). FBR failed $V_{avg} \ge 1.8 \text{ V}$ and startup.
    *   S5: Low frequency (80 Hz). FBR failed stability.
    *   S6: Temperature shift. FBR ok.

    *   FBR (Full-Bridge Rectifier) is simple but inefficient. It has two diode drops (approx 0.5V combined for DSCH at low currents).
    *   For S4 (weak excitation), $V_{oc}$ is lower. The diode drop significantly reduces the voltage delivered to the storage capacitor.
    *   For S3 (strong excitation), there is no voltage regulation, so $V_{out}$ climbs too high.

    *   *Voltage Regulation:* A Zener clamp (DZ33) is needed on the output node to limit $V_{max}$ to 3.3 V.
    *   *Efficiency/Voltage Boost:* To address S2 and S4, we need a more efficient way to extract energy.
    *   *Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI):* This is a classic technique for piezos. It flips the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the voltage swing and improving power extraction.
    *   *Parallel-SSHI or Series-SSHI:*
        *   Parallel-SSHI: An inductor $L$ is switched in parallel with the piezo at the voltage extrema.
        *   Series-SSHI: An inductor is switched in series.
    *   *Simplified SSHI (Standard):* Piezo -> Rectifier -> Storage. An inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are placed in parallel with the piezo to flip the charge.

    *   **Design 1: FBR + Zener Clamp + Storage Capacitor.**
        *   The basic FBR failed S3 ($V_{max}$) and S4 ($V_{avg}$).
        *   Adding a Zener (DZ33) fixes S3.
        *   However, it doesn't solve the efficiency problem of S4.
        *   *Actually*, if S4 fails $V_{avg}$, a simple rectifier might not be enough. But let's try a "regulated FBR" first as a baseline. Wait, the FBR reference results already showed FAIL for S2, S3, S4, S5.

    *   **Design 2: SSHI (Parallel) + FBR + Storage + Zener.**
        *   Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo terminals (pzp, pzn).
        *   The switch $S$ closes at the voltage extrema (zero crossings of $I_p$).
        *   This "flips" the voltage across $C_p$, increasing the energy available to the bridge.
        *   Bridge: DSCH diodes.
        *   Output: $C_{out}$ and DZ33 Zener.

    *   **Design 3: SSHI (with a slightly different arrangement) or a Charge Pump.**
        *   Maybe a Synchronous Rectifier? (Wait, SYNC controllers are available).
        *   A SYNC controller can drive switches. If we replace the diodes with switches, we get a synchronous bridge. However, the SYNC controller here seems designed for the SSHI-style flipping (closes for `ton` at extrema).
        *   Let's check the SYNC spec: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema... edges: 'both', 'pos', 'neg'". This is exactly for SSHI.

    *   Let's refine the Parallel-SSHI (PSSHI) topology:
        *   Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        *   Switch S1 connects pzp and pzn through an inductor L? No, for Parallel-SSHI, the inductor $L$ is in parallel with the piezo, and the switch $S$ closes to create an LC resonant circuit.
        *   Circuit:
            1.  $L$ connected between pzp and a node `mid`.
            2.  Switch $S$ connected between `mid` and pzn.
            3.  SYNC controller $G$ controls $S$.
            4.  Rectifier: D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn). (Wait, the FBR provided in the reference was: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]. This is a standard bridge if pzp/pzn are the AC input).
            5.  Storage $C_{out}$ and Zener $D_{zener}$ (0, out).

    *   *Wait*, let's re-read the FBR provided:
        - `["pzp", "out"]` (Anode pzp, Cathode out)
        - `["pzn", "out"]` (Anode pzn, Cathode out)
        - `["0", "pzp"]` (Anode 0, Cathode pzp)
        - `["0", "pzn"]` (Anode 0, Cathode pzn)
        - This is a bridge. When $V_{pzp} > 0$, D1 conducts. When $V_{pzn} > 0$, D2 conducts. When $V_{pzp} < 0$, D3 conducts. When $V_{pzn} < 0$, D4 conducts. Correct.

    *   *Wait*, the SSHI flip happens at the *voltage peaks*. The SYNC controller closes at the "piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current". This is the correct timing for SSHI.

    *   *Comparing SSHI vs FBR:*
        SSHI increases the voltage across the rectifier, helping S2 and S4.
        The Zener clamp handles S3.
        The large output capacitor handles the ripple and stability (S5).

    *   *Proposed Design 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener*
        *   $L_1$ (pzp, mid)
        *   $S_1$ (mid, pzn) - controlled by $G_1$
        *   $D_1$ (pzp, out), $D_2$ (pzn, out), $D_3$ (0, pzp), $D_4$ (0, pzn) - DSCH
        *   $D_z$ (0, out) - DZ33
        *   $C_{out}$ (out, 0)
        *   $G_1$ (SYNC): edges="both", ton=... (to be optimized), phase=0.

    *   *Proposed Design 2: Half-Bridge SSHI?* (Maybe too complex).
    *   *Proposed Design 3: Simple FBR + Zener + larger Capacitor* (To see if the Zener alone fixes S3 and the Cap fixes S5).
        *   Wait, the FBR failed S2 and S4. Zener and Cap won't fix the low voltage in S2/S4. SSHI is the primary way to fix that.

    *   *Refining Design 1 (Parallel SSHI):*
        Is there a more efficient bridge? A synchronous bridge? But the SYNC controllers are limited to 2, and the SSHI flip already uses one. Using two for the bridge is possible, but the bridge needs to be high-frequency (100Hz) and the SYNC controllers here are for the peaks. A standard diode bridge is fine if we use SSHI to boost the voltage.

    *   *Wait, check "ton" for SSHI:*
        $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        For $L = 10 \text{ mH}$ and $C_p = 25 \text{ nF}$, $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-2} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \times 1.58 \times 10^{-5} \approx 50 \mu \text{s}$.
        This is within the $10^{-7}..10^{-3}$ range.

    *   *Wait, is there a better topology?*
        The "Standard" SSHI is often a *Series* SSHI (where the inductor is in series with the piezo) or *Parallel* SSHI. In Parallel SSHI, the inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with the piezo.
        So: pzp -> L -> mid -> S -> pzn. (This is what I have).
        Alternatively: pzp -> S -> mid -> L -> pzn. (Same thing).

    *   *What about the "vpp <= 0.05 V" requirement?*
        This is quite strict. A large storage capacitor $C_{out}$ will be needed.
        Max value for $C$ is $47 \mu\text{F}$. Let's start with something like $22 \mu\text{F}$.

    *   *Let's double-check the FBR Reference results again:*
        S1: OK
        S2: FAIL $V_{avg}$ (1.76 V < 1.8 V)
        S3: FAIL $V_{max}$ (5.68 V > 3.6 V), FAIL ripple (84 mV > 50 mV)
        S4: FAIL $V_{avg}$ (1.51 V < 1.8 V)
        S5: FAIL settled (dv > 0.02 V)
        S6: OK

        S2 and S4 need more voltage (SSHI).
        S3 needs clamping (Zener).
        S3 and S5 need better smoothing (larger $C_{out}$ and Zener).

    *   Design A: Parallel-SSHI + Full-Bridge + Zener + $C_{out}$
        - L: 10mH
        - S: controlled by SYNC (both edges)
        - Bridge: 4x DSCH
        - Clamp: 1x DZ33
        - Storage: 22uF

    *   Design B: Parallel-SSHI + Half-Bridge + Zener + $C_{out}$
        - (A half-bridge might have lower losses, but a piezo is AC, so it needs a full bridge).

    *   Design C: Just a Full-Bridge + Zener + very large $C_{out}$
        - Let's see if this solves S3, S5. It won't solve S2, S4. But it's a good baseline to check if the Zener alone works. Wait, I should focus on designs that *could* pass all.

    *   Let's try a *modified* SSHI. Instead of a full bridge, can we use a synchronous rectifier?
        - No, only 2 SYNCs available. One for the SSHI flip. One for... what?
        - Maybe use the SYNC to just do a "Half-wave" rectification? No, that's less efficient.

    *   Let's refine the Parallel-SSHI + Full-Bridge.
        - Components: L1, S1, G1, D1, D2, D3, D4, Dz, Cout.
        - Total: 9 components. (Limit is 16).

    *   Wait, is there any risk with the Parallel-SSHI?
        - The switch closes at the peaks. The inductor $L$ and piezo $C_p$ form a resonator. The current oscillates, flipping the voltage on $C_p$. Then the diode bridge captures this increased voltage.
        - The `ton` is critical. $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{L C_p} / 2$? No, for a voltage flip (half-cycle of the LC resonance), it's $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        - Let's check: $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{L C_p}$. Period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L C_p}$. Half period (to flip the voltage) is $\pi\sqrt{L C_p}$.
        - With $L=10\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF}$, $t_{on} \approx 50 \mu\text{s}$.

    *   *Another consideration:* The Zener clamp. DZ33 breaks down at 3.3 V. This will keep $V_{max} \le 3.6 \text{ V}$.

    *   *Wait, if S5 (low frequency) failed "settled",* it might be due to the capacitor being too small or the interaction with the load. A larger $C_{out}$ should stabilize the mean output.

    *   *Self-Correction on the Bridge:*
        The reference bridge:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        Wait, this is a bridge? Let's trace:
        When $V_{pzp}$ is positive and $V_{pzn}$ is negative:
        - D1: pzp(+) -> out(Vout) : Conducts if $V_{pzp} > V_{out} + V_d$
        - D2: pzn(-) -> out(Vout) : No
        - D3: 0 -> pzp(+) : No
        - D4: 0 -> pzn(-) : Conducts if $0 > V_{pzn} + V_d$
        Current path: pzp -> D1 -> out -> load -> 0 -> D4 -> pzn.
        This is a standard full-wave rectifier. (Assuming pzp and pzn are the two terminals of the piezo).
        Wait, if pzp and pzn are the terminals, and it's a current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$, then $V_{pzp}$ and $V_{pzn}$ are not relative to ground?
        Usually, the piezo is modeled as $C_p$ and $I_p$ between pzp and pzn.
        If the bridge is as described, the nodes are:
        - pzp
        - pzn
        - out
        - 0
        Current from piezo (pzp to pzn) flows through D1, load, D4.
        Current from piezo (pzn to pzp) flows through D2, load, D3.
        Yes, this is a full-bridge rectifier.

    *   *Let's check the "S" (switch) again:*
        - `S1: nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC`.
        - `SYNC: closes its switches for "ton" seconds at the piezo voltage extrema`.
        - For Parallel-SSHI: The switch $S_1$ should be in parallel with the piezo.
        - So $S_1$ nodes are `[pzp, pzn]`.
        - *But* we need an inductor $L$ for the LC flip.
        - So the flip path is: pzp -> L1 -> n1 -> S1 -> pzn.
        - Now, when S1 closes, the LC circuit (L1 and $C_p$) resonates.

    *   *Is there a more efficient way to do this?*
        Maybe a "Synchronous" Rectifier using the SYNC controllers?
        - But we need to flip the voltage first (SSHI) to get the voltage up for S2 and S4.
        - Let's stick to Parallel-SSHI + FBR + Zener.

    *   *One more thing:* The storage capacitor $C_{out}$ value.
        - For $V_{pp} \le 0.05 \text{ V}$, we need $C_{out} \approx I_{load} \times \frac{T}{V_{pp}}$.
        - S2: $I_{load} = 1.8\text{V} / 150\text{k}\Omega \approx 12 \mu\text{A}$.
        - $T = 1/100 = 0.01 \text{ s}$.
        - $C_{out} \approx 12 \mu\text{A} \times 0.01\text{s} / 0.05\text{V} = 2.4 \mu\text{F}$.
        - The reference design used $2.2 \mu\text{F}$ and had $V_{pp} = 20 \text{ mV}$ for S2. So $2.2 \mu\text{F}$ is actually enough for S2.
        - But for S3: $I_{load} = 3.3\text{V} / 2200\text{k}\Omega \approx 1.5 \mu\text{A}$. $V_{pp}$ was $84 \text{ mV}$? That's strange. Why would $V_{pp}$ be higher for a lighter load?
        - Ah, maybe the rectifier is not the only source of ripple. In S3, the voltage is much higher, and the energy delivered per cycle is larger. The $V_{pp}$ might be coming from the rectifier's charging spikes.
        - A larger $C_{out}$ (e.g., $10-22 \mu\text{F}$) would help damp those spikes.

    *   Topology 1: Parallel-SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener + Storage Capacitor.
        *   $L_1$: `[pzp, n1]`, $S_1$: `[n1, pzn]`, $G_1$: SYNC (both edges)
        *   $D_1$: `[pzp, out]`, $D_2$: `[pzn, out]`, $D_3$: `[0, pzp]`, $D_4$: `[0, pzn]` (DSCH)
        *   $D_z$: `[0, out]` (DZ33)
        *   $C_{out}$: `[out, 0]`
    *   Topology 2: Parallel-SSHI + Half-Bridge Rectifier + Zener + Storage Capacitor.
        *   (Just in case the full bridge drop is too much, although SSHI should fix that. But a half-bridge only takes half the energy).
        *   Actually, let's try a "Full-Bridge with Zener" and no SSHI as a baseline, just to see the effect of the Zener. (Wait, I can't do that, I already know FBR failed S2 and S4).
    *   Topology 3: A "Modified Parallel-SSHI" where the inductor is in the bridge? (No, that's not standard).
        *   How about an "Inductor-First" SSHI? (L in series with the piezo).
        *   Series-SSHI: The inductor is in series with the piezo and a switch closes to flip the voltage. This is usually more complex.
        *   Let's stick with Parallel-SSHI.

    *   Wait, let me re-verify the Parallel-SSHI switch timing.
        - $V_{piezo}$ is a sine wave.
        - Current $I_p$ is a sine wave.
        - Voltage $V_{piezo}$ peaks when $I_p = 0$.
        - The SYNC controller closes at the "zero crossings of the piezo current".
        - This is exactly when $V_{piezo}$ is at its extrema.
        - Perfect.

    *   *Refining values for the JSON:*
        - $L_1 = 10 \text{ mH}$ (typical)
        - $C_{out} = 22 \mu\text{F}$ (to be safe on ripple)
        - $t_{on} = 50 \mu\text{s}$ (initial guess)
        - $D$ models = DSCH (lowest drop)
        - $D_z$ model = DZ33

    *   *One final check on S3 (Strong excitation, light load):*
        - $I_p = 100 \mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 2200 \text{ k}\Omega$.
        - $V_{oc} \approx 6.4 \text{ V}$.
        - With FBR, $V_{out}$ went to 5.7 V.
        - With the DZ33 Zener, $V_{out}$ will be clamped to $\sim 3.3 \text{ V}$.
        - This should solve $V_{max} \le 3.6 \text{ V}$.

    *   *One final check on S4 (Weak excitation):*
        - $I_p = 30 \mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 1000 \text{ k}\Omega$.
        - $V_{oc} \approx 1.9 \text{ V}$.
        - In FBR, $V_{out}$ was 1.51 V (due to diode drops).
        - With SSHI, the voltage $V_{piezo}$ is effectively boosted, so $V_{out}$ should exceed 1.8 V.
